headline: Rommel retreats at El Alamein
border_caption: Lt. Gen. Bernard Montgomery, commander of Britain’s Eighth Army, watches the battle from the turret of his Grant tank at El Alamein.

image.file: File:Lieutenant General Bernard Montgomery, commanding the British Eighth Army in North Africa, in the turret of his Grant command tank at El Alamein, 5 November 1942. E18980.jpg
image.note: Lt. Gen. Bernard Montgomery in the turret of his Grant command tank at El Alamein, November 5, 1942.

hook: November 4, 1942: Rommel’s army broke at El Alamein. Defying Hitler’s order to stand fast, the “Desert Fox” ordered a retreat that wouldn’t stop until his forces reached Tunisia.
body: For nearly two weeks, Montgomery’s Eighth Army had slugged its way through minefields and gun lines in the Egyptian desert. Hitler’s instructions to Rommel were blunt: show your troops “no other road than that to victory or death.”

By the afternoon of November 4, British armor had broken through, the commander of the Afrika Korps, General Wilhelm Ritter von Thoma, had been captured, and Italian divisions were surrounded. At 5:30 p.m., unable to wait any longer for Hitler’s reply, Rommel ordered the retreat.
Egypt and the Suez Canal were safe, and the desert war had turned for good. Churchill later wrote: “Before Alamein we never had a victory. After Alamein we never had a defeat.”
closer: Rommel or Montgomery: who was the better general? 👇
